problemText: Which of these groups of words is a PHRASE rather than a clause?
choices: the sprinklers turned on at dawn
beside the recycling bins
my sneakers squeaked
the gym smelled like fresh paint
hints: Ask each group two questions: who or what is the doer, and what is the action?
A phrase has no subject-verb pair at all. One of these only tells you WHERE something is, and nobody in it does anything.

problemText: Which of these groups of words is a CLAUSE?
choices: waiting outside the band room for twenty minutes
across the muddy field behind the school
the puppy chewed my shoelace
to return the library books before Friday
hints: A clause needs a subject-verb pair. Hunt for the doer first, because that is the half people forget.
Do not pick the longest one. An -ing word standing alone is not acting as the verb, a to-word is not either, and a location word such as "across" starts a phrase.

problemText: Which of these groups of words is a DEPENDENT clause?
choices: because the sprinklers came on early
under the folding table
the field was still soaked
running through the wet grass
hints: First throw out anything with no subject-verb pair, because a phrase cannot be any kind of clause.
Two options have a pair. Check the very first word of each: a starter word such as because, although, when or since holds the thought open and makes the clause dependent.

problemText: Read this sentence: "The neighbor who waters our plants left a note on the door." Which group of words is the dependent clause?
choices: The neighbor
on the door
left a note on the door
who waters our plants
hints: A dependent clause still needs BOTH halves of the pair. Test each option: who or what, and doing what?
A subject with no verb is not a clause, and a verb with no subject is not one either. Look for the group that has both and opens with who, which or that.

problemText: A student says that "behind the old cafeteria on a rainy Tuesday morning" must be a clause because it is long, and that "Snow fell" must be a phrase because it is only two words. Which labeling is actually correct?
choices: Both of the student's labels are correct.
"Behind the old cafeteria on a rainy Tuesday morning" is a phrase, and "Snow fell" is a clause.
Both groups are phrases, because neither one names a real doer.
Both groups are clauses, because each one describes something that happened.
hints: Length is never the test. Run the subject-verb hunt on each group separately.
The long group stacks up where-and-when details and never says who did anything. In the short group, "snow" is the doer and "fell" is the action.

problemText: Read this sentence: "After the fire drill ended, the students who had left their jackets inside hurried back up the stairs." Which statement about its parts is correct?
choices: "After the fire drill ended" is a dependent clause, and "who had left their jackets inside" is a phrase.
"After the fire drill ended" is a phrase, and "up the stairs" is a dependent clause.
"After the fire drill ended" is an independent clause, and "who had left their jackets inside" is a dependent clause.
"After the fire drill ended" and "who had left their jackets inside" are both dependent clauses, and "up the stairs" is a phrase.
hints: Take the three groups one at a time and run the same test on each: subject, verb, then check the front word.
"The fire drill ended" is a pair held open by "After." In "who had left their jackets inside," who is the doer and had left is the action. "Up the stairs" has no doer at all.

problemText: Which sentence is a COMPOUND sentence?
choices: The bell rang, and everyone grabbed their backpacks.
The bell rang at the end of fourth period.
When the bell rang, everyone grabbed their backpacks.
The bell rang and echoed down the empty hallway.
hints: A compound sentence needs TWO independent clauses, so cover the joining word and check that each side has its own subject and its own verb.
One option has a starter word on the front of its first clause, which makes that clause dependent. Another has one subject doing two things, which is only a compound verb.

problemText: Which sentence is a SIMPLE sentence?
choices: Nadia stayed after school, and Theo walked home alone.
Because Nadia stayed after school, Theo walked home alone.
Nadia stayed after school; Theo walked home alone.
Nadia and Theo stayed after school for the poster contest.
hints: A simple sentence has exactly one independent clause and no dependent clause. Count the subject-verb pairs in each option.
Two names sharing one verb is a compound SUBJECT, and that is still one clause. A semicolon between two complete sentences still makes a compound sentence.

problemText: What type of sentence is this? "Although the forecast promised sun, we packed two umbrellas."
choices: simple
compound
complex
compound-complex
hints: Run the two counts: how many independent clauses, and how many dependent clauses?
"We packed two umbrellas" stands alone, and "Although the forecast promised sun" cannot. One independent plus one dependent has a name.

problemText: Which version combines these two sentences correctly AND signals how the ideas really relate? "The bus broke down on Cypress Road. We walked the last six blocks."
choices: The bus broke down on Cypress Road, but we walked the last six blocks.
The bus broke down on Cypress Road, so we walked the last six blocks.
The bus broke down on Cypress Road, we walked the last six blocks.
The bus broke down on Cypress Road, or we walked the last six blocks.
hints: Name the relationship before you pick a word. Did the breakdown cause the walking, or did the walking happen in spite of it?
But signals contrast, or signals a choice between two things, and a comma with no joining word at all is a comma splice. Only one of these signals a result.

problemText: What type of sentence is this? "When the sprinklers came on, Renata grabbed the picnic blanket, and Owen rescued the paper plates."
choices: compound-complex
complex
compound
simple
hints: Find every subject-verb pair first, then decide which ones could stand alone.
There are three pairs here. One is held open by the starter word "When," and the other two are joined the legal way with a comma plus "and."

problemText: A writer wants to combine these two facts so that the small number of tickets becomes background information and the sell-out is the main point the reader remembers. "The drama club printed only sixty tickets. The winter show sold out in one afternoon." Which version does that?
choices: Although the winter show sold out in one afternoon, the drama club printed only sixty tickets.
The drama club printed only sixty tickets, and the winter show sold out in one afternoon.
Because the drama club printed only sixty tickets, the winter show sold out in one afternoon.
The drama club printed only sixty tickets, the winter show sold out in one afternoon.
hints: Whatever sits in the independent clause is what the reader walks away with, so decide which fact belongs in the dependent clause.
One option pushes the sell-out into the background instead, one gives both facts equal weight in two independent clauses, and one joins two complete sentences with only a comma.

problemText: Which group of words is a FRAGMENT?
choices: The gym doors were locked.
We waited outside for ten minutes.
Because the gym doors were locked.
Someone finally found the custodian.
hints: Run the three-part test on each one: subject, verb, finished thought.
Three of these finish their thought. One has a subject and a verb but a starter word is holding it open, so you are left waiting.

problemText: What is wrong with this sentence? "The power went out during third period, the whole school got an early lunch."
choices: It is a comma splice - two complete sentences held together by only a comma.
It is a fragment - it is missing a subject.
It is a run-on - the two complete sentences have nothing at all between them.
Nothing is wrong with it.
hints: Cover each side of the comma and read what is left. Could each half be sent as its own message?
Both halves are complete sentences, and there IS a mark between them - just not a strong enough one. That error has its own name.

problemText: Which revision correctly fixes this sentence? "My dog hates thunder, he hides under the kitchen table."
choices: My dog hates thunder he hides under the kitchen table.
My dog hates thunder, however, he hides under the kitchen table.
My dog hates thunder, then he hides under the kitchen table.
My dog hates thunder, so he hides under the kitchen table.
hints: There are exactly three legal fixes: a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus one of for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.
Deleting the comma is not a fix - it turns the splice into a run-on. However and then are not joining words, so a comma in front of either one repairs nothing.

problemText: Which revision fixes the fragment AND punctuates the result correctly? "While my sister practiced her trumpet. I moved my homework to the basement."
choices: While my sister practiced her trumpet; I moved my homework to the basement.
While my sister practiced her trumpet, I moved my homework to the basement.
While my sister practiced her trumpet, and I moved my homework to the basement.
While my sister practiced her trumpet I moved my homework to the basement.
hints: Read the first group alone. "While" holds it open, so it is a dependent clause and it has to lean on the complete sentence beside it.
A semicolon needs a complete sentence on its LEFT, and a joining word is only for two independent clauses. A dependent clause that comes first attaches with a comma after it.

problemText: Which sentence is written correctly?
choices: Our science teacher collects rain in a barrel, she uses it for the courtyard garden.
Our science teacher collects rain in a barrel she uses it for the courtyard garden.
Even though our science teacher collects rain in a barrel. She still waters the courtyard garden with a hose.
Our science teacher collects rain in a barrel; she uses it for the courtyard garden.
hints: Three of these commit one of the three errors from this lesson. Test both halves of every option: complete sentence, or not?
One joins two complete sentences with only a comma, one joins them with nothing at all, and one strands an "Even though" clause as its own sentence.

problemText: A student wrote this: "The trail was closed for repairs, therefore we hiked the loop by the creek instead." Which revision fixes the error?
choices: The trail was closed for repairs; therefore, we hiked the loop by the creek instead.
The trail was closed for repairs therefore we hiked the loop by the creek instead.
The trail was closed for repairs, therefore, we hiked the loop by the creek instead.
The trail was closed for repairs, therefore; we hiked the loop by the creek instead.
hints: Check both halves first. If each one could stand alone, ask what is actually holding them apart.
"Therefore" is a transition word, not a joining word, so no arrangement of commas around it can hold two sentences apart. Something stronger has to sit at the boundary.

problemText: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
choices: After we finished the mural we cleaned the brushes, the trays, and the sink.
After we finished the mural, we, cleaned the brushes, the trays, and the sink.
After we finished the mural, we cleaned the brushes the trays and the sink.
After we finished the mural, we cleaned the brushes, the trays, and the sink.
hints: Two comma jobs are in play here: closing an introductory element, and separating items in a series.
The setup "After we finished the mural" needs a comma after it, the three things cleaned need commas between them, and nothing at all is allowed to sit between "we" and "cleaned."

problemText: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
choices: My uncle Desmond who repairs pianos drove up from Macon.
My uncle Desmond, who repairs pianos, drove up from Macon.
My uncle Desmond, who repairs pianos drove up from Macon.
My uncle Desmond who repairs pianos, drove up from Macon.
hints: Run the removal test. Lift out "who repairs pianos" and read what is left. Does the sentence still work, and do you still know exactly who drove up?
His name is already in the sentence, so the piano part is extra information - and extra information takes a PAIR of commas. One comma on its own builds half a fence.

problemText: None of these sentences has a comma before the word "and," but exactly one of them needs one. Which sentence needs a comma before "and"?
choices: Trevor grabbed his helmet and rode down to the courts.
Trevor grabbed his helmet and his elbow pads before he left.
Trevor grabbed his helmet and Elena checked the tire pressure on both bikes.
Trevor and Elena rode down to the courts after dinner.
hints: A comma goes before a joining word only when it is holding two complete sentences together. Cover the "and" and test what follows it.

In three of these, the part after "and" has no subject of its own - it is a second verb, a second object, or a second name sharing one verb. Only one option has a whole new subject and verb after the "and."

problemText: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
choices: It was a damp, chilly morning, so Priya wore her dark blue hoodie.
It was a damp chilly morning, so Priya wore her dark blue hoodie.
It was a damp, chilly morning, so Priya wore her dark, blue hoodie.
It was a damp chilly morning, so Priya wore her dark, blue hoodie.
hints: Every option punctuates the two complete sentences the same way, so the adjectives are what decide this. Run the "and" test on each pair, then swap their order.

"Damp and chilly" works and "chilly, damp morning" works, so that pair is coordinate and needs a comma. "Dark and blue" does not work and "a blue dark hoodie" does not either, so that pair gets nothing.

problemText: Which sentence is written correctly?
choices: The team lost it's captain to a sprained ankle, so two seventh grader's stepped in.
The team lost its captain to a sprained ankle, so two seventh grader's stepped in.
The team lost its captain to a sprained ankle, so two seventh graders stepped in.
The team lost it's captain to a sprained ankle, so two seventh graders stepped in.
hints: Two apostrophe rules are being tested at once. Expand the first one to check it, and ask what job the second one could possibly be doing.
"It's" means "it is," and "the team lost it is captain" falls apart - so the possessive here is "its," with no apostrophe. And an apostrophe never makes a word plural.

problemText: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
choices: On the first cold morning of November, Ms. Kaplan our homeroom teacher, brought in a box of donated gloves.
On the first cold morning of November, Ms. Kaplan, our homeroom teacher, brought in a box of donated gloves.
On the first cold morning of November Ms. Kaplan, our homeroom teacher, brought in a box of donated gloves.
On the first cold morning of November, Ms. Kaplan, our homeroom teacher, brought in a box of donated gloves, everyone took a pair.
hints: Three separate checks: is the introductory element closed off, is the extra information fenced on BOTH sides, and does the sentence stop where the thought stops?

"Our homeroom teacher" can be lifted straight out, so it needs a comma before and after. One option leaves the setup phrase open, and one keeps going past the end of the thought with only a comma holding two complete sentences apart.
